title: Pacific Western Airlines 3801
summary: Pacific Western Airlines Flight 3801, a Boeing 707 cargo flight carrying 86 cattle and 5 crew, crashed on approach to Edmonton on January 2, 1973, killing all on board. The flight had become fatigued after traveling from Athens with stops at Tenerife, Santa Maria, and Moncton, with a relief crew taking over in Moncton. During descent from 35000 feet, the crew reported a failure in the number 4 generator. At landing, the first officer at the controls initiated a go-around but at 90% engine power the aircraft impacted the ground in a nose-up attitude with landing gear and flaps down. The investigation found the crew was heavily fatigued, the first officer was inexperienced, and may have reverted to Boeing 737 procedures, and previous recording on the flight data recorder had ceased a week before the accident.
probable_cause: Crew fatigue combined with first officer's inexperience and possible use of incorrect procedures during go-around, resulting in failure to successfully climb away from terrain.

factors.evidence: Crew failed to get sufficient sleep during transition in Moncton, accumulating fatigue from long international flight segments.
First officer had only 2800 total flight hours and 1200 on type; flight was his last check ride to be certified as first officer.
Multiple demands during go-around with engine failure on descent and lack of FDR data from week prior to accident affected crew performance.
Aircraft attempted go-around with pitch angle +8 degrees but impacted ground at 90% engine power.

title: Aeroflot 141
summary: Aeroflot Flight 141, a Tupolev Tu-154 with 100 occupants, crashed 1.5 kilometers short of runway 25 at Prague Ruzyně Airport on 19 February 1973. The aircraft descended below minimum safe altitude during approach and struck terrain. While most passengers initially survived the impact, a post-impact fire destroyed the fuselage and killed 62 passengers and 4 crew members. The crew reported passing the outer marker but failed to arrest descent at the required 1240 feet altitude.

title: Aeroflot 630
summary: An Ilyushin Il-18V operating Aeroflot Flight 630 from Dushanbe to Moscow via Leninabad crashed on 24 February 1973, killing all 79 occupants including five children. The aircraft climbed to 6,600 meters and was supposed to turn 60 degrees right toward Leninabad but instead turned only 10 degrees right, maintaining that course for three minutes with autopilot engaged. The autopilot was subsequently disengaged and the aircraft began a series of escalating bank angles, entering a steep left spiral at 90 degrees bank with vertical speeds of 100 meters per second, ultimately disintegrating from high dynamic loads at 2,200 meters altitude.

title: Invicta International Airlines 435
summary: The aircraft approached Basel during a heavy snowstorm that reduced visibility significantly. title: 1973 Sunnyvale mid-air collision
summary: On 12 April 1973, a NASA Convair CV-990 and a US Navy Lockheed P-3 Orion collided on approach to Moffet Field, California in good weather with great visibility. The approach controller cleared the CV-990 for approach to runway 32R, then three minutes later cleared it to approach runway 32L, the same runway where the P-3 was conducting touch-and-go landings. The CV-990 crew did not question this runway assignment change. At 300 feet altitude, the P-3 initiated a climb, colliding with the CV-990 which was descending above it. Both aircraft crashed on Sunnyvale Municipal Golf Course, killing all 11 on the CV-990 and 5 of the 6 on the P-3.

title: Aeroflot 6551

title: Aeroflot 512
summary: An Aeroflot Tupolev Tu-134A aborted takeoff at Amman-Marka International Airport while accelerating through rotation speed, apparently due to a perceived engine failure. The aircraft descended below the glide slope and crashed in a wooded ravine 2 miles short of the runway. Witnesses reported the aircraft ascending to 400-500 feet then rapidly descending to 200 feet before striking trees. The severe downdraft associated with the thunderstorm, combined with the crew's decision to continue the approach into the known storm, resulted in the crash.
probable_cause: Severe downdraft encountered on approach combined with the captain's decision to continue into a known severe storm area. Contributing factors included lack of timely warning about storm severity from weather service and improper storm assessment by dispatcher.

title: TWA 742
summary: On 28 August 1973, TWA Flight 742, a Boeing 707 en route from Honolulu to Los Angeles during descent to FL110, experienced severe pitch oscillations over the Pacific Ocean. The aircraft underwent 50 abrupt pitch-up and pitch-down cycles in approximately 2 minutes, generating 2.4g peak acceleration forces. Investigation discovered that the left elevator had excessive waviness (0.42 inches) and was misaligned relative to the right, requiring different control forces. Unaware the aircraft was out of trim, the crew's descent control inputs triggered a classic pilot-induced oscillation. Two crew members and three passengers were injured; one critically injured passenger died two days later of intracranial bleeding.
probable_cause: Excessive waviness and misalignment of the left elevator relative to the right, combined with out-of-trim condition undetected by the crew, caused pilot-induced oscillation during descent when crew over-corrected control inputs attempting to level the aircraft.

factors.evidence: The upper skin of both elevators experienced waviness due to compression, with wave amplitude excessive: 0.42 inches for the left elevator and 0.32 for the right, and the left elevator deflected significantly further than the right with the same control column deflection.
With no one realizing it, when the accident 707 was expected to be properly trimmed, it was in fact flying slightly out of trim.

The crew used the amount of force and forward deflection of the control column that they were accustomed to on other 707s; on this particular aircraft, this amount of force was too great and deflected the elevator much more than the crew intended, pushing the aircraft into a violent downward pitch. Trying to rectify that, they pulled the yokes back, over-corrected, and caused yet another violent pitch-up instead of leveling off.
The 707 entered a violent porpoising motion, alternating abrupt pitch-up and pitch-down movement with 50 oscillations in about 2 minutes and peak acceleration forces of 2.4g.

events.text: Crew cleared to descend to FL 110; pilots disconnected the autopilot, reduced power and entered a descent from FL330.
As the 707 descended through 22,000 feet at 350 knots indicated airspeed, the nose abruptly pitched up; out-of-trim condition caused by excessive elevator waviness triggered pitch excursion.

Crew tried to level the aircraft but nose rapidly pitched down; pilots reduced engine power to idle, disengaged rudder power, Mach trim and yaw damper; aircraft entered violent porpoising with 50 oscillations in 2 minutes, 2.4g peak acceleration.
Oscillations gradually abated; crew regained level flight at 19,500 feet and continued descent to Los Angeles.

title: JAT Airways 769

title: Aeroflot 964
summary: The Tu-104 crashed during approach to Moscow. Navigation instruments failed and the crew lost spatial orientation. Multiple navigation instruments including the compass and artificial horizon failed. The crew lost spatial orientation in poor visibility and were unable to determine aircraft position or attitude. With correct right bank only putting the plane into a sharp left bank that reached 70 degrees, the aircraft crashed in a field 16 km northwest of Domodedovo Airport.
probable_cause: Multiple navigation instruments including the compass and artificial horizon failed. When the plane banked slightly to the right, the pilots corrected the right bank only to put the plane into a sharp left bank that reached 70 degrees, causing the crash.

title: 1973 Rome airport attack and hijacking
summary: On December 17, 1973, armed members of Fatah conducted a terrorist attack at Rome-Fiumicino Airport, firebombing Pan Am Flight 110 while at the gate. The airport's inadequate security design and staffing allowed gunmen to penetrate to the aircraft tarmac with automatic weapons and incendiary grenades. Fires from grenades destroyed the aircraft and killed thirty persons on board, with evacuation hampered by gunmen obstructing emergency exits. The attack exposed fundamental deficiencies in airport security infrastructure and regulatory oversight.

title: Iberia Airlines 933
summary: On approach to Boston, Iberia 933 encountered low-level wind shear that increased the descent rate beyond crew recognition. The DC-10 collided with approach light piers 500 feet short of the runway, breaking the right main landing gear. The aircraft became airborne again and landed on the runway safely, with all 168 on board surviving though 13 were injured. The investigation found that inadequate monitoring combined with marginal visual cues and lack of wind shear information prevented the captain from arresting the excessive descent rate.
